When you design a system with caching, the big question is:



How do we keep cache and database in sync?


That’s where Read-Through and Write-Through caches come in. They are required to solve consistency, performance, and simplicity problems.

In modern systems, databases are slow compared to in-memory caches, so caching is used to improve performance. However, using a cache introduces challenges like data consistency and added complexity in managing reads and writes.
blocks.text:
When you design a system with caching, the big question is:



How do we keep cache and database in sync?


That’s where Read-Through and Write-Through caches come in. They are required to solve consistency, performance, and simplicity problems.

In modern systems, databases are slow compared to in-memory caches, so caching is used to improve performance. However, using a cache introduces challenges like data consistency and added complexity in managing reads and writes.

blocks.content: 1. Read-through caching

In cache-aside, the application checks the cache, goes to the DB on a miss, and stores the result. In read-through, that miss-handling logic is built into the cache layer itself. The app only ever calls the cache it never touches the DB directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124482-796705129.png
App only talks to cache layer, it never directly talks to database. Cache handles everything internally.
When app calls get, cache first checks if data exists.

["If data is present, it returns immediately.
","If data is missing, cache itself fetches from database.
"]
items: If data is present, it returns immediately.
If data is missing, cache itself fetches from database.

blocks.content: Then it stores the result in cache and returns it. App does not know whether it was a hit or miss.
This is read-through caching where cache manages miss logic. In cache-aside, app handles miss, fetch and store logic itself.
Use when: you want caching to be invisible to application code. Common with ORM-level caches and managed services like AWS ElastiCache or DAX (DynamoDB Accelerator).
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279679459-930699590.png
blocks.alt: On a cache miss the cache layer itself fetches from the DB, stores it, and returns the data

blocks.content: 2. Write-through caching
Every write goes to both the cache and the database synchronously. The write is only confirmed when both succeed. The cache is always in sync reads after a write never see stale data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785399124482-336843540.png
App writes data to both cache and database at the same time. Write is successful only when both cache and DB succeed.
This keeps cache always in sync with database. After a write, all reads hit cache and get fresh data.
There is no stale data problem. But writes become slower because two systems must succeed.

["If one fails, you need rollback handling. Safer approach is writing to database first, then updating cache.
","If cache write fails, data is still safe in DB and cache will fix later via TTL.
"]
items: If one fails, you need rollback handling. Safer approach is writing to database first, then updating cache.
If cache write fails, data is still safe in DB and cache will fix later via TTL.

blocks.content: Use when: reads follow writes frequently and staleness is unacceptable user settings, permissions, pricing. Often combined with read-through so both reads and writes go through the cache layer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785279684731-240992485.png
blocks.alt: The safer write-through order writes the database first, then updates the cache

blocks.content: Read-through vs write-through vs cache-aside

["Read-throughCache fetches from DB on miss app never touches DB directly.
","Write-throughEvery write updates cache and DB together always consistent.
","Cache-asideApp manages everything check cache, miss → fetch DB, populate cache manually.
"]
items: Read-throughCache fetches from DB on miss app never touches DB directly.
Write-throughEvery write updates cache and DB together always consistent.
Cache-asideApp manages everything check cache, miss → fetch DB, populate cache manually.

blocks.content: Read-through + write-through together = the cache handles all reads and writes transparently. The app only ever calls the cache the cache layer owns the relationship with the DB.
Short and focused only what wasn't already covered:

• Read-through the key difference from cache-aside is that the cache handles the miss itself, the app never touches the DB. Diagram + code showing the contrast clearly.
  • Write-through both writes happen simultaneously, cache stays always in sync. Safe version (DB first) vs parallel version.
  • 3-line comparison at the bottom showing all three side by side so the distinction is crystal clear.
